\chapter{Five Short Answers --- Agreed, Sure, True, Exactly, Of Course}
\label{ch:respuestas-cortas}
\hlchaptermodality{284}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer someone in Spanish with a single short phrase, and say what is inside each one.}

Complete ES-C284-por-supuesto: give all five answers in order, and name the Latin verb inside each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[de acuerdo]{de acuerdo — hearts brought together}

\label{lesson:ES-C284-de-acuerdo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: how many new words were in \emph{no hay de qué}? (None.) And what does \emph{mil} mean? (A thousand.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sí — the shortest answer of all, which you have.
  \item no hay de qué — another formula assembled from small pieces.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de a-CUER-do}, stress on the \emph{cuer}. The \emph{ue} is one glide, not two vowels taken in turn. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{de acuerdo} — \textquotedblleft{}agreed.\textquotedblright{}

From \textbf{acordar}, and inside it Latin \textbf{cor}, \textbf{cordis}, the heart. To \emph{acordar} is to bring hearts together.

English has the whole family and rarely notices the organ in it. An \textbf{accord} is this word. \textbf{Concord} is hearts together and \textbf{discord} hearts apart. To \textbf{record} is to bring back to the heart — because the Romans located memory there, so recording was memorising long before it was writing anything down. Even \textbf{courage} is \emph{cor} with a French ending on it.

The stressed \emph{o} of \emph{cordis} opens into \emph{ue}, the change you have watched happen again and again: \emph{cor} to \emph{cuerdo}, as \emph{portam} went to \emph{puerta}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now agree without saying \emph{sí}.

That matters more than it sounds. \emph{Sí} answers a question; \emph{de acuerdo} accepts a proposal. Conversations run on the second one far more than on the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de acuerdo}
  \item \emph{sí}, then \emph{de acuerdo}, and hear the difference in what each answers
  \item \emph{de acuerdo, gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is inside \emph{acuerdo}? (\emph{Cor}, the heart.) Why does \emph{record} belong to it? (To bring back to the heart — where memory was thought to sit.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[seguro]{seguro — without a care, which came to mean reliable}

\label{lesson:ES-C284-seguro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what is inside \emph{acuerdo}? (\emph{Cor}, the heart.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item de acuerdo — the answer before this one.
  \item bien — another one-word answer you already give.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{se-GU-ro}, stress in the middle. The \emph{gu} before \emph{r} is a hard \emph{g}; the \emph{u} here is fully pronounced. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{seguro} — \textquotedblleft{}sure,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}safe.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{securus}: \emph{se-}, without, plus \textbf{cura}, care. Free of care. The Romans meant untroubled; Spanish and English both dragged it towards reliable, which is a different thing.

English took it twice, and the two arrivals do not look alike. \textbf{Secure} came late and whole, out of a book. \textbf{Sure} came early through French, worn down to one syllable, having lost the \emph{c} on the road. The same Latin word walked in through two doors.

\textbf{Cura} itself is in English \textbf{cure}, \textbf{curator} and \textbf{curious} — all of them about taking care of something, or taking rather too much.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Se-} is another dial worth keeping.

It means without or apart, and it is doing the same job in \emph{seguro} that \emph{sub-} did in \emph{sonrisa}: a small piece in front changing the whole. You are collecting prefixes now, not only words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{seguro}
  \item \emph{seguro} and \emph{secure}, and hear one word twice
  \item \emph{de acuerdo}, then \emph{seguro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{securus}? (\emph{Se-}, without, and \emph{cura}, care.) Which English word is the worn-down one? (\emph{Sure}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cierto]{cierto — what has been sifted out}

\label{lesson:ES-C284-cierto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what are the two pieces of \emph{securus}? (\emph{Se-}, without, and \emph{cura}, care.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item seguro — the answer before this one, and a near neighbour in meaning.
  \item la puerta — where you first watched a stressed \emph{o} open into \emph{ue}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CIER-to}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is the \emph{th} of \emph{think} in much of Spain and an \emph{s} elsewhere. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cierto} — \textquotedblleft{}true,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}certain.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{certus}, and it is a participle: from \textbf{cernere}, to sift, to separate, to decide. What is \emph{certus} is what has been sifted out from everything it was mixed up with.

The English family is large and the sieve is invisible in all of it. \textbf{Certain} is this word. To \textbf{discern} is to sift apart. To be \textbf{concerned} is to be sifted together with something. And a \textbf{secret} is \emph{se-cernere}, a thing sifted aside — the same \emph{se-} you met in \emph{seguro}, one word ago.

The stressed \emph{e} opens into \emph{ie} here, as it did in \emph{puerta} with an \emph{o}: \emph{certus} to \emph{cierto}. Two vowels, one habit.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Certainty is a metaphor, and a physical one.

Sifting, separating, deciding: the Romans had one word for all three, and every English word about being sure still has grain and a sieve at the bottom of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cierto}
  \item \emph{es cierto}
  \item \emph{seguro}, then \emph{cierto}, and hear which agrees with a person and which with a fact
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{cernere} mean? (To sift.) What is a \emph{secret}, taken apart? (Something sifted aside.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[exacto]{exacto — driven out, then weighed out}

\label{lesson:ES-C284-exacto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cernere} mean? (To sift.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cierto — the answer before this one.
  \item sí — the plain agreement these are all sharpening.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{e-XAC-to}, stress in the middle. The \emph{x} here is \emph{ks}, said fully: \emph{ek-SAK-to}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{exacto} — \textquotedblleft{}exactly,\textquotedblright{} used on its own as an answer.

Latin \textbf{exactus}, the participle of \textbf{exigere}: \emph{ex-}, out, plus \textbf{agere}, to drive. To drive out; then to demand; then to weigh out precisely, because a Roman checking a coin was driving the true amount out of the metal.

\textbf{Agere} is everywhere in English: an \textbf{act}, an \textbf{agent}, an \textbf{agenda} — things to be driven along. \textbf{Exigent} kept the demanding sense unchanged.

As an answer, \emph{exacto} is the one that agrees with a detail rather than with a person. Somebody has got a number or a name right, and you are confirming the number, not backing the speaker.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four answers, and each agrees with something different.

\emph{De acuerdo} accepts a plan, \emph{seguro} backs a person, \emph{cierto} confirms a fact, \emph{exacto} confirms a detail. English leans on one word for all four and lets the tone carry it; Spanish would rather you chose.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{exacto}
  \item \emph{cierto}, then \emph{exacto}
  \item the four in order — \emph{de acuerdo}, \emph{seguro}, \emph{cierto}, \emph{exacto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the pieces of \emph{exigere}? (\emph{Ex-}, out, and \emph{agere}, to drive.) What does \emph{exacto} agree with? (A detail, not a person.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[por supuesto]{por supuesto — it was under the conversation already}

\label{lesson:ES-C284-por-supuesto}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what does \emph{exacto} agree with? (A detail.) And what did \emph{cernere} mean? (To sift.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item exacto — the answer before this one.
  \item la sonrisa — where you first met \emph{sub-} doing its work.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{por su-PUES-to}, stress on the \emph{pues}. Another \emph{ue} glide, and the \emph{s} stays clear throughout. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{por supuesto} — \textquotedblleft{}of course.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Supuesto} is the participle of \textbf{suponer}, Latin \textbf{supponere}: \emph{sub-}, under, plus \textbf{ponere}, to place. Something \emph{supuesto} has been placed underneath — assumed, taken as given, sitting under the conversation without ever being said out loud.

English \textbf{suppose}, \textbf{supposition} and \textbf{presuppose} are that same placing. And English's own \textquotedblleft{}of course\textquotedblright{} is doing something similar with a different picture: the thing runs along the expected course, so nobody had to steer it.

There is \emph{sub-} again, and you met it turning a laugh into a smile. Prefixes are worth more than words. One of them unlocks dozens.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five answers: \emph{de acuerdo}, \emph{seguro}, \emph{cierto}, \emph{exacto}, \emph{por supuesto}.

Three of the five are participles — \emph{acuerdo} aside, they name a state something has been put into. Spanish keeps reaching for the finished action when it wants a short answer, and now you have five examples instead of one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{por supuesto}
  \item \emph{sub-} and \emph{supuesto}, and hear the prefix
  \item all five in order — \emph{de acuerdo}, \emph{seguro}, \emph{cierto}, \emph{exacto}, \emph{por supuesto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the pieces of \emph{supponere}? (\emph{Sub-}, under, and \emph{ponere}, to place.) Where did you meet \emph{sub-} before? (Inside \emph{sonrisa}, turning a laugh down.) And what is inside \emph{acuerdo}? (\emph{Cor}, the heart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
